entries.title: 2WP - TWO-WAY PEG
51% ATTACK
entries.body:
A hypothetical scenario on the Bitcoin system in which a malicious actor controls more than 50% of the total mining computing power (*hashrate*). With such dominance, the attacker can manipulate the consensus process, enabling malicious actions such as double spending, where the same bitcoins are spent a first time on a chain that is ultimately made obsolete, then a second time on the valid chain. Another goal of a 51% attack is transaction censorship. However, carrying out a 51% attack requires considerable financial, human, energy, and technical resources, and makes the malicious actor liable to be discovered before the attack takes place. Although theoretically possible, a 51% attack on Bitcoin is considered very unlikely due to the decentralization of mining and the large amount of computing power currently deployed.

*This attack is also called the "Goldfinger Attack".*

entries.title: ACINQ
entries.body: French company specializing in the development of solutions for the Lightning Network. ACINQ is the originator of Eclair, a major implementation of the Lightning protocol written in Scala. The company also develops Phoenix, a *self-custodial* mobile wallet that integrates a Lightning node directly on the user's phone. ACINQ also operates one of the largest Lightning nodes on the network.

entries.title: ADAPTOR SIGNATURE
entries.body:
A cryptographic method that makes it possible to combine a real signature with an additional signature (called an “adaptor signature”) to reveal a secret piece of data. This method works such that knowing two of the three elements among the valid signature, the adaptor signature, and the secret makes it possible to deduce the missing third one. One of the interesting properties of this method is that if we know our peer's adaptor signature and the specific point on the elliptic curve linked to the secret used to compute this adaptor signature, we can then derive our own adaptor signature that will correspond to the same secret, without ever having had direct access to the secret itself. In an exchange between two parties who do not trust each other, this technique allows a simultaneous revelation of two sensitive pieces of information between the participants. This process eliminates the need for trust in instantaneous transactions such as a coinswap or an Atomic Swap. Let's take an example to understand it well. Alice and Bob wish to send each other 1 BTC each, but they do not trust each other. They will therefore use adaptor signatures to eliminate the need for trust toward the other party in this exchange (it is therefore an “atomic” exchange). They proceed as follows:
* Alice initiates this atomic exchange. She creates a transaction `m_A` that sends 1 BTC to Bob. She creates a signature `s_A` that validates this transaction using her private key `p_A` (`P_A = p_A \cdot G`), and using a nonce `n_A` and a secret `t` (`N_A = n_A \cdot G` and `T = t \cdot G`): 
```math
s_A = n_A + t + H(N_A + T \parallel P_A \parallel m_A) \cdot p_A
```
* Alice computes the adaptor signature `s_A'` from the secret `t` and her real signature `s_A`:  
```math
s_A' = s_A - t
```
* Alice sends Bob her adaptor signature `s_A'`, her unsigned transaction `m_A`, the point corresponding to the secret `T`, and the point corresponding to the nonce `N_A`. We call this information an “adaptor”. Note that with just this information, Bob is not able to recover Alice's BTC.
* However, Bob can verify that Alice is not trying to cheat him. To do so, he verifies that Alice's adaptor signature `s_A'` does indeed correspond to the promised transaction `m_A`. If the following equation holds, then he is convinced that Alice's adaptor signature is valid: 
```math
s_A' \cdot G = N_A + H(N_A + T \parallel P_A \parallel m_A) \cdot P_A
```
* This verification gives Bob guarantees from Alice, such that he can continue the atomic exchange process with peace of mind. He will then in turn create his own transaction `m_B` sending 1 BTC to Alice and his own adaptor signature `s_B'`, which will be linked with the same secret `t` that only Alice knows for the moment (Bob does not know this value `t`, but only its corresponding point `T` which Alice provided to him): 
```math
s_B' = n_B + H(N_B + T \parallel P_B \parallel m_B) \cdot p_B
```
* Bob sends Alice his adaptor signature `s_B'`, his unsigned transaction `m_B`, the point corresponding to the secret `T`, and the point corresponding to the nonce `N_B`. Alice can now combine Bob's adaptor signature `s_B'` with the secret `t`, which only she knows, in order to compute a valid signature `s_B` for the transaction `m_B` that sends her Bob's BTC: 
```math
s_B = s_B' + t
```
```math
(s_B' + t) \cdot G = N_B + T + H(N_B + T \parallel P_B \parallel m_B) \cdot P_B
```
* Alice broadcasts this signed transaction `m_B` on the Bitcoin blockchain in order to recover the BTC that Bob promised her. Bob becomes aware of this transaction on the blockchain. He is therefore able to extract the signature `s_B = s_B' + t` from it. From this information, Bob can isolate the famous secret `t` that he needed:
```math
t = (s_B' + t) - s_B' = s_B - s_B'
```
* Now, this secret `t` was the only piece of information Bob was missing to produce the valid signature `s_A`, from Alice's adaptor signature `s_A'`, which will allow him to validate the transaction `m_A` that sends one BTC from Alice to Bob. He then computes `s_A` and in turn broadcasts the transaction `m_A`: `s_A = s_A' + t`
```math
(s_A' + t) \cdot G = N_A + T + H(N_A + T \parallel P_A \parallel m_A) \cdot P_A
```

entries.title: ADDR
entries.body: A network message formerly used on Bitcoin to communicate the addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections. This old format, limited to 128 bits per address, was only suited to IPv6, IPv4, and Tor version 2 addresses. In the face of the arrival of new protocols such as Tor V3 and the need for better extensibility for future network protocols, the `addr` format was superseded by `addrv2`, introduced in BIP-0155.

entries.title: ADDR.DAT
entries.body: Name of the old file used in Bitcoin Core to store information about the network's peers (that is, nodes) with which the user's node has interacted or could potentially interact. This file has been replaced by the `peers.dat` file since version 0.7.0.

entries.title: ADDRESS SPOOFING
entries.body:
An attack in which a malicious actor creates an address (or any other payment identifier) that closely resembles the victim's. The goal is to trick the user into copying this wrong address during a transaction, which leads to the bitcoins being sent to the attacker instead of the intended destination. 

The attacker exploits the user's haste, as they may copy the wrong address if they carry out their transaction without precisely verifying its accuracy. In general, to set up this attack, the attacker makes small payments to the victim's wallet in order to insert the fake address into their transaction history. This attack is rather used with altcoins, where it is common to reuse the same receiving addresses, unlike Bitcoin, where using fresh addresses for each transaction is a more widespread practice. However, Bitcoin users are not immune to this attack.

Another method of putting the wrong address in front of the victim is the use of fraudulent wallet management software that imitates legitimate software, or the modification of the address when a machine is compromised, between the moment it is copied and the moment the transaction is built. This is then sometimes called “*address swapping*”.

To protect against these various attack methods, it is important to verify several characters of the address, especially at the level of its *checksum* (at the end), on the screen of the signing device before signing the transaction.

*This attack is also sometimes referred to as Address Poisoning.*

entries.title: ADDRMAN
entries.body:
A Bitcoin Core module that manages the addresses of known peers on the network. It maintains two in-memory tables: the “new” table, which contains addresses that have been discovered but not yet tested (1024 buckets of 64 entries), and the “tried” table, which contains addresses to which the node has already successfully connected (256 buckets of 64 entries). These tables are serialized in the `peers.dat` file.

The module was introduced by Pieter Wuille in 2012, replacing the previous system that stored addresses in `addr.dat` without any bucketing structure. Its operation was strengthened by the addition of *feeler connections* and the *test-before-evict* mechanism, which make it possible to verify the reachability of addresses before promoting or evicting them.

entries.title: ADDRV2
entries.body: An evolution of the `addr` message on the Bitcoin network, proposed with BIP-0155. The `addr` message was used to broadcast the addresses of nodes that accept incoming connections, but it was limited to 128-bit addresses. This size was adequate for IPv6, IPv4, and Tor V2 addresses, but insufficient for other protocols. The updated version `addrv2` is designed to support longer addresses, notably 256-bit Tor V3 hidden services, as well as other network protocols such as I2P or future protocols.

entries.title: AEZEED
entries.body:
A recovery phrase format specific to LND, used to generate and back up the private keys of the *onchain* wallet associated with a Lightning node. Like BIP-0039, aezeed produces a 24-word mnemonic phrase, but it fixes two major limitations of that standard: the absence of versioning and the absence of the wallet's creation date.

The basis of an aezeed phrase is 19 bytes long, with: 1 byte of version (allowing the wallet to know how to re-derive the addresses), 2 bytes of timestamp expressed in days since the Bitcoin genesis block (which covers dates up to 2188), and 16 bytes of entropy used to derive the *seed*. The timestamp tells the software from when to scan the blockchain.

These 19 bytes are encrypted with AEZ, an AEAD scheme resistant to *nonce* reuse, using a key derived by Scrypt (`n=32768`, `r=8`, `p=1`) from an optional passphrase (by default: the string “aezeed”). The 33-byte ciphertext is encoded into 24 words via the same list as BIP-0039. Unlike BIP-0039, the mnemonic phrase is itself a ciphertext, and it is possible to change the passphrase or update the encryption parameters without generating new keys.

entries.title: AGORISM
entries.body: A political philosophy founded by Samuel Edward Konkin III in the 1970s. It is an extension of libertarianism, emphasizing direct action to break free from the yoke of state authority through counter-economics, an economic practice that takes place outside the frameworks regulated by the government. Agorist ideology rests on natural law theory, which asserts that individuals' natural rights are superior to laws imposed by the State. This includes the primacy of private property, respect for physical integrity, and the freedom to contract. Agorists reject any form of traditional political participation such as voting, which they consider a validation of the State's coercive authority. They aspire to a society where economic and social exchanges take place freely in an open market, called the Agora, thus aiming at a peaceful revolution to gradually erode the power of the State. Their emblem is, moreover, “A3”, for “Agora, Anarchy, Action”. The principle of agorism is described in the *New Libertarian Manifesto* published in 1980. This paper is built upon Murray Rothbard's *Libertarian Manifesto*, but it goes even further. Many bitcoiners claim to be agorists and think that Bitcoin is the perfect tool for it.

entries.title: AIR COOLING
entries.body: A cooling system used for ASICs in the context of Bitcoin mining. *Air cooling* consists of using fans to dissipate the heat generated by the components. Ambient air is drawn in to cool the chips before being expelled. This cooling method is the most widespread, because the fans are present directly on the machines when purchased. It is generally the least expensive to acquire, but it is less efficient compared to techniques such as *hydro cooling* or *immersion cooling*.

entries.title: AIR-GAPPED
entries.body:
Describes a computing device that is physically isolated from any network, including the Internet, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any other wired or wireless connection. In the context of Bitcoin, an air-gapped device is used to secure private keys by keeping them away from any online attack vector.

The principle is simple: if a device is never connected to a network, it becomes extremely difficult for an attacker to access it remotely to extract sensitive information. An air-gapped *hardware wallet* signs transactions offline. Data is exchanged with the Internet-connected computer by a physical means, typically via a microSD card or a QR code, without ever establishing a direct connection.

This approach represents one of the highest levels of security for storing bitcoins. Devices such as the Coldcard, Foundation Devices' Passport, or Blockstream's Jade offer this mode of operation.

entries.title: ALBY
ALBY HUB
entries.body: Open-source application that lets you run a personal Lightning Network node and connect it to various applications via the Nostr Wallet Connect (NWC) protocol. Alby Hub is installed on a personal server, a computer, or in the cloud, and serves as a control center for the user's Lightning payments. Alby Hub is non-custodial: the user keeps their private keys and full control of their funds. It uses an LDK (*Lightning Development Kit*) implementation to manage the Lightning node.

entries.title: ALERT SYSTEM
entries.body:
A historical Bitcoin mechanism that made it possible to broadcast emergency messages to all the nodes of the network. Introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in version v0.3.10, shortly after the *value overflow incident* of August 2010, this system was used to warn node operators in the event of a critical bug or a network problem.

Alerts were relayed through Bitcoin's peer-to-peer network, in the same way as transactions and blocks. Only messages signed with a specific ECDSA private key were considered valid. This key was initially held by Satoshi alone, then shared with a few developers such as Gavin Andresen. In the early versions (up to v0.3.20), a valid alert triggered a "*safe mode*" that automatically disabled the RPC commands related to transactions, which gave its holders considerable power over the network.

Because of the risk of centralization and the possibility of abusive uses, the system was gradually abandoned: the code was removed in Bitcoin Core v0.13.0, and a final "Alert Key Compromised" alert was broadcast to permanently invalidate any future message. The private key was then made public in 2018.

entries.title: ALGORITHM
entries.body: A finite and unambiguous sequence of instructions for carrying out a task. In the context of computer science, it is a process written in a programming language that tells a computer how to carry out a mission.

entries.title: ALTCOIN
entries.body: Refers to any cryptocurrency other than bitcoin (BTC). The term "altcoin" is the contraction of "alternative" and "coin" (alternative coin). Some maximalist bitcoiners also use the term "shitcoins" to refer to altcoins.

entries.title: ALUVM
entries.body: Acronym for "*Algorithmic Logic Unit Virtual Machine*". A register-based virtual machine specifically designed for the deterministic execution of distributed computing tasks and the validation of *smart contracts*, notably within the framework of RGB contracts. AluVM was initially developed by Dr Maxim Orlovsky and is currently maintained by the LNP/BP Standards association.

entries.title: AMBOSS
entries.body: Amboss is a Lightning Network analytics and monitoring platform, founded in 2021 by Jesse Shrader and Anthony Potdevin. It provides detailed data on the network topology, nodes, channels, and liquidity flows, allowing node operators to optimize their management. Amboss also offers Magma, a marketplace dedicated to Lightning liquidity, where operators can buy and sell channel capacity.

entries.title: AML - ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING
entries.body: Refers to the set of procedures, laws, and regulations intended to prevent money laundering. These rules require financial institutions such as bitcoin exchange platforms to actively monitor their customers' transactions, carry out identity checks, keep records, and report suspicious activity to the authorities.

entries.title: ANCESTOR MINING
entries.body: Another name sometimes given to CPFP (*Child-Pay-For-Parent*). Ancestor mining is the principle whereby a miner does not choose a transaction solely on the basis of its own transaction fees, but also takes into account the fees of the ancestor transactions.

entries.title: ANCHOR
ANCHOR OUTPUTS
entries.body: A proposal that aims to improve the management of transaction fees in Lightning channels. At each state change in a Lightning channel, the stakeholders create and sign a new commitment transaction that reflects the new distribution of funds within the channel. The problem with this mechanism lies in determining the transaction fees at the time of its creation. Indeed, transaction fees on the Bitcoin network are subject to strong fluctuations, both upward and downward. If the fees set for the last commitment transaction are insufficient at the time of the unilateral closing of the channel, not only will the transaction take a considerable time to confirm, but the time-locking mechanisms (*timelocks*) could also allow funds to be stolen. *Anchor outputs* make it possible to reserve a small portion of the funds in a commitment transaction to cover future fees. In the event of network congestion and rising fees, *anchor outputs* make it possible to modify the transaction fees after the commitment transaction has been created, thus ensuring a sufficiently fast closing of the Lightning channel.

entries.title: ANCHORS.DAT
entries.body: A file used in the Bitcoin Core client to store the IP addresses of the outbound *block-relay-only* nodes to which a client was connected before being shut down. `anchors.dat` is therefore created each time the node is stopped and deleted when it is restarted. The nodes whose IP addresses are contained in this file are used to help quickly establish connections when the node restarts.

entries.title: ANNEX
entries.body:
An optional field reserved in the witness structure (*witness*) of SegWit v1 (Taproot) inputs, defined by BIP-0341. The annex occupies the last position in the witness stack and is distinguished by a `0x50` prefix. Although it currently has no function assigned by the consensus rules, this space was provided for from the very design of Taproot to accommodate future extensions of the protocol.

An important property of the annex is that any Taproot or Tapscript signature must commit (*commit*) to its value when it is present. This means that an attacker cannot add, modify, or remove an annex without invalidating all the signatures of the input concerned. This cryptographic guarantee ensures that the annex cannot be exploited to alter a transaction that has already been signed.

entries.title: ANONSETS - ANONYMITY SETS
entries.body:
Anonsets serve as indicators for evaluating the degree of privacy of a particular UTXO. More specifically, they measure the number of indistinguishable UTXOs within the set that includes the coin under study. Since a group of identical UTXOs is needed, anonsets are generally calculated within a cycle of coinjoins. They make it possible, where relevant, to judge the quality of coinjoins. A large anonset means an increased level of anonymity, because it becomes difficult to distinguish a specific UTXO within the set. Two types of anonsets exist:
* The forward anonymity set;
* The backward anonymity set.

The first indicates the size of the group among which the UTXO under study is hidden at the output, given the input UTXO. This indicator makes it possible to measure the resistance of the coin's privacy against an analysis going from past to present (input to output). In English, the name of this indicator is "*forward anonset*", or "*forward-looking metrics*".

![Diagram of the forward anonset calculation over three successive coinjoin mixes, totaling 13 indistinguishable UTXOs.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/anonsets-anonymity-sets/assets/image-1.png)

The second indicates the number of possible sources for a given coin, given the output UTXO. This indicator makes it possible to measure the resistance of the coin's privacy against an analysis going from present to past (output to input). In English, the name of this indicator is "*backward anonset*", or "*backward-looking metrics*".

![Backward anonset, which traces back from a coinjoin to its ancestor inputs stage by stage up to the genesis coinjoin.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/anonsets-anonymity-sets/assets/image-2.png)

*In French, it is generally accepted to use the term "anonset". However, it could be translated as "ensemble d'anonymat" or "potentiel d'anonymat". In both English and French, one also sometimes speaks of a "score" to refer to anonsets (forward score and backward score).*

entries.title: ANTI-EXFIL SIGNING
entries.body:
A signing protocol that prevents a compromised hardware wallet from leaking the user's private key through the signatures it produces. In the ECDSA or Schnorr signature scheme, each signature requires a random nonce. A malicious device can manipulate this nonce to discreetly encode information about the private key in it, an attack known as a "covert channel" (*covert channel*) attack. The Dark Skippy attack notably showed that it is possible to extract an entire HD seed with only two signatures.

The anti-exfiltration protocol (also called "anti-kleptography") relies on an exchange of nonce contributions between the host (the wallet software) and the hardware wallet. The host first provides a random value to the hardware signer, which must incorporate it into the computation of its nonce. The final nonce therefore results from the combination of the two contributions, which prevents either party from controlling it alone. Thanks to a cryptographic commitment, the host can verify that its contribution was indeed taken into account in the signature produced.

This mechanism is implemented in hardware wallets such as the BitBox02 and Blockstream's Jade. It is an essential defense against supply chain attacks, where a device's firmware could have been modified before delivery.

entries.title: ANTPOOL
entries.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in 2014 by Bitmain Technologies, the leading manufacturer of ASIC mining hardware. Based in China, Antpool regularly ranks among the largest mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It offers several payout methods and caters to individual miners and professional mining infrastructures alike.

entries.title: AOPP
entries.body:
Acronym for "*Address Ownership Proof Protocol*". It is a controversial protocol, designed to automatically prove ownership of Bitcoin addresses. This mechanism allows users to demonstrate that they control a specific address, directly through their compatible wallet software. Initially, AOPP was created to simplify the verification of address ownership, a legal requirement for customers wishing to transfer their bitcoins off exchange platforms in certain jurisdictions, such as Switzerland.

Nevertheless, this protocol was the subject of significant criticism within the Bitcoin community, because it could set a precedent where users would have to ask for permission to exercise their right of ownership over their own funds (*self-custody*). Faced with this criticism, many wallet software projects chose not to adopt this protocol.

entries.title: APERTURE
entries.body:
An HTTP 402 reverse proxy developed by Lightning Labs, designed to enable paid access to web services via the Lightning Network. Concretely, Aperture sits in front of a web server or an API and requires a Lightning micropayment before authorizing access to the requested resource.

Aperture relies on the L402 protocol (*Lightning HTTP 402*), which combines the HTTP 402 status code ("Payment Required"), macaroons, and the Lightning Network to create an authentication and payment standard on the web. When a client sends a request to a protected resource, Aperture responds with a 402 code accompanied by a macaroon and a Lightning invoice. Once the payment is made, the client obtains a preimage which, combined with the macaroon, forms a valid L402 token. This token then serves as both authentication and proof of payment for subsequent requests.

Aperture supports proxying of gRPC (HTTP/2) and REST (HTTP/1 and HTTP/2) requests. It also includes a *rate limiting* system per token or per IP address, based on a *token bucket* algorithm. Used in production notably by Lightning Loop, Aperture illustrates a vision of the web where micropayments replace traditional subscription or advertising models to monetize APIs and online services.

entries.title: API
entries.body: Acronym for "*Application Programming Interface*". In the general context of computer science, an API is a set of rules and specifications that software can follow to communicate with each other. They allow developers to access features or data of an application, an operating system, or another service for their own software.

entries.title: APO - ANYPREVOUT
entries.body: Name given to BIP-0118, which proposes adding two new modifier SigHash Flags, named `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` and `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT`. The term "*AnyPrevOut*" comes from the contraction of "*Any Previous Output*", which could be translated into French as "toute sortie précédente".

entries.title: AQUA
entries.body: A mobile wallet developed by JAN3, available on iOS and Android, designed to simplify the use of Bitcoin, the Lightning Network, and the Liquid network in a single application. Aqua allows you to send and receive bitcoins on-chain or on the Liquid sidechain. For Lightning payments, Aqua uses atomic swaps, which allows it to do without an embedded Lightning node while keeping custody of the funds at all times.

entries.title: ARBITRAGE
entries.body: The practice of exploiting differences in the price of BTC (or any other asset) between different exchange platforms to make a profit. Arbitrage involves buying bitcoin on a platform where the price is relatively low and simultaneously selling it on another platform where the price is higher. Price gaps can arise because of differences in liquidity, demand, trading volumes and transfer times between exchange platforms. Arbitrage helps to balance prices across different platforms.

entries.title: ARK
entries.body:
A joinpool-type upper-layer protocol on Bitcoin, proposed by Burak Keceli in May 2023 and implemented from 2024 by Ark Labs. Ark makes it possible to share on-chain UTXOs between multiple users via *Virtual Transaction Outputs* (VTXOs) in order to improve Bitcoin's scalability.

The protocol is built around *Ark Service Providers* (ASPs), operators who periodically organize “rounds” during which users' VTXOs are consolidated and anchored in new on-chain Bitcoin transactions. This mechanism prevents any fractional reserve. Transfers between users of the same ASP are fast, inexpensive and offer privacy comparable to that of a coinjoin. “Out-of-round” payments are also possible for immediate settlement, at the cost of temporary trust in the ASP and the sender.

The protocol is non-custodial, but VTXOs expire after a defined period. If the user does not show up before expiry, the ASP can recover the liquidity. The user retains the ability to perform a unilateral on-chain exit at any time.

The version implemented without covenants, called *clArk*, emulates spending conditions through n-of-n multisignatures between the participants of a round, at the cost of overhead in bandwidth and storage. Adding covenants to Bitcoin would improve scalability and reduce the required interactivity. Ark is complementary to the Lightning Network and interoperable via gateways.

entries.title: ASCII
entries.body: Acronym for “*American Standard Code for Information Interchange*”. It is a character encoding system for computers. The ASCII standard uses 7 bits to represent 128 different characters: uppercase and lowercase letters of the Latin alphabet, digits, punctuation symbols, and control commands, such as the line break or the tab.

entries.title: ASHIGARU
entries.body: A privacy-oriented mobile Bitcoin wallet, forked from the Samourai Wallet code after the seizure of its servers by US authorities in April 2024. Ashigaru carries over Samourai's privacy-protection features, notably Whirlpool coinjoins, Stonewall transactions, collaborative transactions (Stowaway, StonewallX2), ricochets and advanced UTXO control. The project is maintained by an open-source community that continues to develop these privacy tools.

entries.title: ASIC
frenchAliases: CIRCUIT INTÉGRÉ SPÉCIFIQUE À UNE APPLICATION
entries.body: An ASIC is an electronic component designed to perform a specific function with optimal efficiency. In the context of Bitcoin mining, ASICs are specialized integrated circuits that perform hashing operations at high speed and low power consumption. They specialize in running the `SHA256` hash function used in the proof-of-work mechanism. The ASIC is originally the name of the chip. By extension, the acronym “ASIC” often also refers to the machine that houses this chip. Thus, computers specialized in Bitcoin mining are sometimes called “ASICs”, or “miners”. ASICs have gradually replaced other mining methods, such as the use of processors (CPUs) and graphics cards (GPUs), because of their superior energy efficiency and much higher hashrate.

entries.title: ASIC RESISTANCE
entries.body:
A property of a mining algorithm that aims to limit the advantage of application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) over consumer hardware, such as processors (CPUs) or graphics cards (GPUs). The goal is to maintain decentralization of mining by preventing a situation where only actors with expensive, specialized hardware can participate effectively in block validation.

To achieve this resistance, some alternative cryptocurrencies use hash functions that require a lot of random-access memory (*memory-hard*), such as Scrypt or Ethash, which makes ASIC manufacturing harder or less advantageous. The idea is that if the algorithm demands varied resources (memory, bandwidth, computation), an ASIC does not offer as clear a performance gain as for a simple algorithm like SHA-256.

In the case of Bitcoin, ASIC resistance has never been a goal. Bitcoin uses SHA-256, a function that lends itself very well to hardware optimization. The Bitcoin network therefore saw ASICs appear as early as 2013, which gradually made CPU and GPU mining unprofitable. ASIC resistance remains a subject of debate: its supporters see it as a guarantee of decentralization, while its critics point out that it merely delays hardware specialization without ever durably preventing it.

entries.title: ASICBOOST
entries.body:
An algorithmic optimization method invented in 2016, designed to increase Bitcoin mining efficiency by about 20% by reducing the amount of computation needed for each header hashing attempt. This technique exploits a peculiarity of the SHA256 hash function, used for mining, which splits data into chunks before processing it. AsicBoost keeps one of these chunks unchanged across several hashing attempts, which allows the miner to perform only part of the work for this chunk over several attempts. This data sharing allows results of previous computations to be reused, thereby decreasing the total number of computations needed to find a valid hash.

AsicBoost can be used in two forms: Overt ASICBoost and Covert ASICBoost. The Overt AsicBoost form is visible to everyone, because it involves using the block's `nVersion` field as an additional nonce. The Covert form seeks to hide these modifications by using Merkle trees. However, this second method has no longer been effective since SegWit because of the second Merkle tree, which multiplies the number of computations needed to use it.

To summarize, AsicBoost makes it possible to avoid performing a full SHA256 for every hashing attempt, because part of the result remains unchanged, which speeds up the miners' work.

entries.title: ASMAP
entries.body: A tool invented by Gleb Naumenko and used by Bitcoin Core to improve the security and topology of the Bitcoin network by diversifying connections between nodes. It is a map from IP addresses to autonomous system numbers (ASNs), allowing a better distribution of outbound connections based on the ASN rather than on IP prefixes. This helps prevent Eclipse attacks (notably the Erebus attack) by making it harder for an attacker to monopolize a target node's connections via IP addresses belonging to the same autonomous system.

entries.title: ASP - ARK SERVICE PROVIDER
entries.body:
An operator of the Ark protocol, responsible for managing VTXOs and for periodically anchoring transactions on the Bitcoin blockchain. The ASP organizes “rounds” (every 15 to 60 minutes depending on configuration) during which users' VTXO transactions are consolidated and recorded *on-chain*, preventing any fractional reserve.

The ASP is *non-custodial*: it does not directly hold users' funds and therefore cannot steal them. However, if a user does not connect during the expiry period of their VTXOs (typically 4 weeks), the ASP can recover the associated liquidity. This model orients Ark toward everyday payments rather than long-term storage. The ASP also ensures interoperability with the Lightning Network via gateways, allowing Ark users to send and receive Lightning payments.

ASPs are by nature larger than *Lightning Service Providers* (LSPs), which could encourage a certain centralization of the system. To mitigate this risk, ASPs can be federated or operate peer-to-peer. For institutions or large bitcoin holders, operating an ASP is a yield opportunity with a minimum of required trust, by providing the liquidity needed by the protocol.

entries.title: ASSET ID
entries.body:
A unique 32-byte identifier assigned to each asset issued via the Taproot Assets protocol. The *asset ID* is produced by hashing with SHA-256 five concatenated elements: the outpoint of the genesis transaction (the one that creates the asset), a tag chosen by the issuer (for example the hash of a brand name), the hash of the metadata associated with the asset (links, images, documents), the index of the output containing the Taproot Assets *commitment* in the genesis transaction, and the type of the asset (normal or *collectible*).

```
asset_id=sha256(genesis_outpoint‖asset_tag‖asset_meta_hash‖output_index‖asset_type)
```

Since it depends on the genesis outpoint, the *asset ID* is globally unique: two distinct issuances will always produce different identifiers. It serves as a key to find an asset in a *Universe*, verify its provenance and distinguish the different types of assets committed in the same *Sparse Merkle Sum Tree*.

entries.title: ASSET MERGE
entries.body: An operation that consists of combining two Taproot Assets assets of the same type into one within a single Taproot output. During an *asset merge*, assets coming from distinct Taproot outputs are grouped into a single *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* committed in a new transaction. The total sum at the root of the tree then reflects all of the merged assets. This operation is the inverse of an *asset split*. It makes it possible to consolidate balances fragmented after several receipts and to simplify the management of a holder's asset tree.

entries.title: ASSET PROOF
entries.body: A cryptographic proof that makes it possible to verify the existence, ownership and provenance of an asset issued via the Taproot Assets protocol. An *asset proof* contains the asset script as well as the path in the *Sparse Merkle Sum Tree* leading to the leaf of the relevant holder. The recipient can partially reconstruct the tree, tweak the issuer's public key and verify that the genesis transaction does exist on the Bitcoin blockchain.

entries.title: ASSET SPLIT
entries.body: An operation that consists of dividing a Taproot Assets asset into two parts distributed across distinct Taproot outputs. The sender updates the *Merkle-Sum Sparse Merkle Tree* of their own output by reducing their balance, then the recipient builds a second tree committed in a new Taproot output containing the received assets. Each transfer of assets between holders relies on this splitting mechanism. Asset proofs (*asset proofs*) must trace back to the genesis transaction to attest to the provenance of the assets after each *split*. It is the inverse operation of an *asset merge*.

entries.title: ASSIGNMENT
entries.body:
In the logic of the RGB protocol, an Assignment is the equivalent of a transaction output that modifies, updates or creates certain properties within the state of a contract. An Assignment has two elements:
* A Seal Definition (the reference to a specific UTXO);
* An Owned State (the data describing the state associated with this new holder).

An Assignment therefore indicates that a portion of the state (for example, an asset) is now allocated to a particular holder, identified via a Single-use Seal linked to a UTXO.

entries.title: ASSUME UTXO
entries.body:
A feature of the main Bitcoin Core client that allows a newly initialized node (which has not yet done the IBD) to defer verification of the transactions and of the UTXO set before a given snapshot. The concept relies on the use of a UTXO set (list of all UTXOs existing at a given moment) loaded by the user via the RPC command `loadtxoutset` and presumed accurate after verification of its cryptographic fingerprint against a hash hardcoded in Core, which allows the node to be synchronized very quickly on the chain with the most accumulated work. Since the node skips the long IBD step, it is very quickly functional for its user. Assume UTXO splits synchronization (IBD) into two parts:
* First, the node performs the *Header First Sync* (verification of headers only) and it considers valid the UTXO set whose fingerprint matches the hash hardcoded in Core;
* Then, once it is functional, the node will verify the complete block history in the background, updating a new UTXO set that it will have verified itself. If the latter does not match the initially loaded UTXO set, it will provide an error message.

Assume UTXO therefore speeds up the preparation of a new Bitcoin node by deferring the verification process of the transactions and of the UTXO set thanks to a snapshot whose hash is hardcoded in Core.

entries.title: ASSUME VALID
entries.body:
A configuration parameter in the main Bitcoin Core client that allows a newly initialized node (which has not yet done the IBD) to skip signature verification for all transactions included in blocks prior to a certain given block. This famous block is defined by the fingerprint of its header, that is to say its hash. The chosen block is renewed with each new version of Bitcoin Core. At initialization, since this parameter is enabled by default, the node will therefore verify the chain of block headers to find the branch with the most accumulated work. If the node detects the hash provided by Core in the branch it has retained, it will omit signature verification for the prior blocks. Otherwise, the node will carry out a traditional synchronization (IBD) to verify everything by itself.

The goal of Assume Valid is to speed up the initial synchronization process of a node without compromising security, by assuming that the majority of the network has already validated these transactions in the past. The only real trade-off for the node is that in the event of a prior theft of bitcoins, it will not be warned. However, it can still make sure of the correctness of the quantity of bitcoins issued. Nodes continue to verify the signatures of transactions after the Assume Valid block. This approach rests on the assumption that if a transaction has been accepted by the network for long enough without challenge, it is unlikely to be fraudulent.

entries.title: ASYNC PAYMENTS
entries.body:
A mechanism that makes it possible to send a Lightning payment to a recipient who is not online at the time of sending. On the classic Bitcoin network, transactions are naturally asynchronous since the recipient does not need to be connected to receive funds. By contrast, the Lightning protocol normally requires the receiver to be online to reveal the secret (the preimage) that finalizes the payment via an HTLC.

This constraint poses a significant problem for mobile wallets, which are not permanently connected. Several approaches have been proposed to solve this limitation. The most promising relies on the use of PTLCs (*Point Time-Locked Contracts*) combined with static BOLT-12 invoices, which allow the payer to build a valid payment without prior interaction with the recipient. Another approach uses trampoline relay nodes: a trusted intermediate node holds the payment until the recipient reconnects, then forwards it to them.

Concrete implementations have emerged, notably in LDK and Eclair. LDK has integrated asynchronous payment logic on the client side and the server side, while Eclair makes it possible to wake up a disconnected mobile peer to forward a pending payment to it. These advances are essential to make Lightning truly usable on mobile devices, where permanent connectivity cannot be guaranteed.

entries.title: ATH - ALL-TIME HIGH
entries.body: Refers to the highest level ever reached by the item under study. Often, ATH refers to the highest price level of bitcoin compared with a state-issued currency over a given period.

entries.title: ATLC
entries.body: Acronym for "*Anchor Timelock Contracts*". It is a conditional payment used within the Ark protocol to provide an atomic payment schedule to a hub, by means of connectors that make it possible to form what is called a "txlock". The purpose of an ATLC is substantially the same as that of an HTLC on Lightning.

entries.title: ATOMIC MULTI-PATH PAYMENTS
entries.body:
An improved version of MPPs (*Multi-Path Payments*) in which each payment fragment has a distinct partial secret, which ensures that the transaction is settled atomically, that is, in full or not at all. 

MPPs are payment techniques on Lightning that make it possible to split a transaction into several smaller parts in order to route them through different paths. In other words, each fraction of the payment takes a different path of nodes. This makes it possible to work around the liquidity limitations of a single channel in the route. In basic MPPs, each payment fraction shares the same secret, and therefore the same hash in the HTLCs. This can make the transaction traceable if an observer is present on several routes, because they can link all these identical secrets together. Moreover, because the secret is the same for all fractions of the payment, the payment is not atomic. This means that some parts of the payment can be executed successfully, while others can fail.

In AMPs, unique partial secrets are used for each fraction. Once all the fragments are received, they allow the recipient to reconstruct the original overall secret and claim the entire payment. This method makes partial settlement of the payment impossible, because possession of all the partial secrets is necessary to unlock the complete payment. This ensures that the payment either fully succeeds or fully fails (that is, it is atomic). AMPs also improve privacy, because there are no longer any visible links between the different routes.

An advantage of AMPs is that they work even if only the receiver and the sender have implemented this method. Intermediate nodes process these payments as regular transactions using HTLCs, without being aware that they are processing fractions of a larger payment.

*"Atomic Multi-Part Payment" is also sometimes used to refer to this same method.*

entries.title: ATOMIC SWAP
entries.body:
A technology enabling an exchange of cryptocurrencies directly between two parties, without the need for trust and without requiring an intermediary. These exchanges are called "atomic" because they can only have two outcomes:
* Either the exchange succeeds and both participants have effectively exchanged their cryptocurrencies;
* Or the exchange fails and both participants walk away with their original cryptocurrencies.

Atomic Swaps can be carried out either with the same cryptocurrency, in which case they are also called "*coinswaps*", or between different cryptocurrencies. Historically, they relied on "*Hash Time-Locked Contracts*" (HTLCs), a time-locking system that guarantees the exchange is either completed or fully cancelled, thus preserving the integrity of the funds of the parties involved. This method required protocols capable of handling both scripts and timelocks. However, in recent years, the trend has moved toward the use of *Adaptor Signatures*. This second approach has the advantage of dispensing with scripts, which thus reduces operational costs. Its other major strength lies in the fact that it does not require the use of an identical hash for both legs of the transaction, which avoids revealing a link between them.

entries.title: AUTOLOOP
entries.body: A feature of Lightning Loop that automates *Loop In* and *Loop Out* operations based on predefined thresholds. The operator of a Lightning node configures inbound and outbound liquidity limits for their channels, and Autoloop automatically triggers *submarine swaps* when these thresholds are exceeded. This makes it possible to maintain a liquidity balance without manual intervention, which is particularly useful for routing nodes that must constantly adjust the distribution of their funds between channels in order to maximize routing revenue.

entries.title: AVERAGE ROUND DURATION
entries.body:
The average round duration is an indicator used to estimate the time a mining pool needs to find a block, based on the network difficulty and the pool's hashrate. It is calculated by taking the number of shares expected to find a block and dividing it by the pool's hashrate. For example, if a mining pool has 200 miners, and each generates an average of 4 shares per second, the pool's total computing power is 800 shares per second:

```text
200 * 4 = 800
```

Assuming that, on average, 1 million shares must be produced to find a valid block, the pool's *Avg. Round Duration* will be 1,250 seconds, or about 21 minutes:

```text
1 000 000 / 800 = 1 250
```

In practical terms, this means that on average, the mining pool should find a block roughly every 21 minutes. This indicator fluctuates with variations in the pool's hashrate: an increase in hashrate reduces the *Avg. Round Duration*, while a decrease lengthens it. It will also fluctuate with each periodic change in Bitcoin's difficulty target (every 2016 blocks). This measure does not take into account blocks found by other pools and focuses solely on the internal performance of the pool under study.

entries.title: BEARER ASSET
entries.body:
A good or financial instrument whose ownership is determined solely by physical possession, without requiring a centralized registry, an intermediary, or a registration in a name. Whoever holds the asset is its legitimate owner. Banknotes, gold coins, and bearer bonds are examples of bearer assets.

This type of asset offers the advantage of not depending on any third party to validate or authorize a transfer of ownership. It gives its holder direct sovereignty, but also implies a responsibility: loss or theft results in the permanent loss of the asset.

Bitcoin in *self-custody* is a digital bearer asset. Possession of the private keys that secure bitcoins confers exclusive control over those funds, without any bank, institution, or centralized registry being involved.

entries.title: BITCOIN ADDRESS
CHAIN ANALYSIS
DIFFICULTY ADJUSTMENT
entries.body:
The difficulty adjustment is a periodic process that redefines the difficulty target for the proof-of-work mechanism (mining) on Bitcoin. This event occurs every 2016 blocks (approximately every two weeks). It increases or decreases the difficulty factor (also called the difficulty target), depending on how quickly the last 2016 blocks were found. The adjustment aims to keep a stable and predictable block production rate, at a frequency of one block every 10 minutes, despite variations in the computing power deployed by miners. The change in difficulty during the adjustment is limited to a factor of 4. The formula executed by nodes to calculate the new target is as follows:
```math
N = A \cdot \left(\frac{T}{1\,209\,600}\right)
```
Where:
* `N`: the new target;
* `A`: the old target;
* `T`: the time elapsed between the first and last block of the period, in seconds;
* `1\,209\,600`: the target time in seconds for 2016 blocks at 10-minute intervals (`2016 \times 600`).

Due to an off-by-one bug introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto, `T` actually measures the duration of 2015 block intervals, and not 2016. The calculation indeed compares the timestamp of the first block of the period (block `n`) to that of the last one (block `n + 2015`), which covers only 2015 intervals. A correct calculation would have compared the last block of the previous period (block `n - 1`) to the last block of the current period (block `n + 2015`), i.e., 2016 intervals. This bug introduces a bias of approximately 0.05% toward a difficulty slightly too high compared to what it should be. It is above all the reason the *time warp* attack is feasible, because retarget periods do not overlap.

*In French, the term “reciblage” is also sometimes used to refer to the adjustment.*

entries.title: FINNEY ATTACK
entries.body:
A type of double spend that targets zero-confirmation transactions. The attacker, who must be a miner, pre-mines a block containing a transaction from their address A to another address B that they also control. Instead of broadcasting this block, they make a payment from that same address A to a merchant's address C. The merchant sees the transaction in the mempool, detects no conflict, and delivers the goods. The attacker then broadcasts their pre-mined block: the transaction to B is confirmed, while the payment to C is invalidated.

Hal Finney described this attack in 2011 on the BitcoinTalk forum. It differs from the 51% attack because it does not require a majority of computing power: it is enough for the attacker to find a block, even with a modest hashrate. In return, its execution window is narrow and it only works against merchants who accept payments without waiting for a confirmation.

entries.title: MERKLE TREE
entries.body:
A Merkle Tree is a cryptographic accumulator. It is a method for proving that a given piece of information belongs to a larger set. It is a data structure that makes it easier to verify information in a compact format. In the Bitcoin system, Merkle trees are used to group and condense the transactions of a block into a single hash, called the Merkle root (or “*Root Hash*”). Each transaction is hashed, then adjacent hashes are hashed together hierarchically until the Merkle root is obtained.

![Complete Merkle tree over 8 transactions, from the leaves TX 1 to TX 8 up to the root HASH 1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/arbre-de-merkle/assets/image-1.png)

This structure makes it possible to quickly verify whether a specific transaction is included in a given block without having to analyze all of the transactions. For example, if I only have the Merkle root and I want to verify that the `TX 7` is indeed part of the tree, I will only need the following proofs:
* `TX 7`;
* `HASH 8`;
* `HASH 5-6`;
* `HASH 1-2-3-4`.
Thanks to this small amount of information, I am able to calculate the intermediate nodes up to the Merkle root.

![Merkle proof for TX 7, with the necessary nodes HASH 8, HASH 5-6 and HASH 1-2-3-4 highlighted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/a/arbre-de-merkle/assets/image-2.png)

Merkle trees are notably used for light nodes (known as “SPV”) that only keep block headers, but not transactions. This structure is also found in the UTREEXO protocol, a protocol for condensing the nodes' UTXO set, and in the Taproot MAST.

*The Merkle tree is named after Ralph Merkle, a cryptographer who designed this structure in 1979. A Merkle tree can also be called a “hash tree”. In English, it is called a “Merkle Tree” or “Hash Tree”.*

entries.title: STATIC ADDRESS
entries.body:
In the context of Silent Payments, designates a unique identifier that makes it possible to receive payments without producing address reuse, without interaction, and without a visible on-chain link between the various payments and the static address. This technique eliminates the need to generate new fresh receiving addresses for each transaction, which avoids the usual interactions in Bitcoin where the recipient must provide a new address to the payer. It is somewhat the equivalent of the reusable payment code in the context of BIP-0047.

This address is composed of two public keys: `B_{scan}` for scanning and `B_{spend}` for spending, concatenated to form the static address `B\ =\ B_{scan}\ \Vert\ B_{spend}`. The recipient publishes this address, allowing senders to derive unique payment addresses without any additional interaction with the recipient. To manage several distinct payment sources, a label can be added to `B_{spend}`, thus creating several labeled static addresses (from `B_1`, `B_2`, etc.). This makes it possible to segregate payments while using a single base address, thus reducing the workload for scanning the blockchain. However, all of an entity's static addresses can easily be associated because of the common use of `B_{scan}`.
